title: India World Cup Winner Dares Selectors to Drop Rohit Sharma: 'Himmat Hai Toh Drop Karo'
excerpt: A former Indian cricketer's bold defense of Rohit Sharma's place in the team adds fuel to the ongoing debate over the veteran opener's future after a lean patch.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • A former World Cup winner challenges selectors to drop Rohit Sharma amid his poor form.
  • Rohit Sharma, 39, is still India's ODI and Test captain despite recent struggles.
  • Debate over Rohit's future intensifies with younger batsmen vying for positions.
  • Rohit's leadership has kept India as the top-ranked ODI side.
  • The BCCI faces a dilemma balancing legacy and team evolution.

The question of Rohit Sharma's future in the Indian cricket team has been simmering for months. A former World Cup-winning teammate has now turned the heat up on the selectors themselves, issuing a blunt dare: "Himmat hai toh drop karo" — if you have the courage, drop him.

The Challenge

The bold statement reflects a broader tension in Indian cricket. Rohit Sharma, 39, has had an undeniable lean patch by his exceptional standards. His recent international scores have fallen short of the runs that built his reputation as one of the greatest white-ball batsmen in history — the only player with three ODI double centuries.

> **"Dropping the captain of a side that reached the 2023 World Cup final and won the 2024 T20 World Cup is a decision no selection panel wants to make unless absolutely necessary."** https://youtube.com/watch?v=CDq7cODy3X0

But form is temporary, and stature casts a long shadow. Dropping the captain of a side that reached the 2023 World Cup final and won the 2024 T20 World Cup is a decision no selection panel wants to make unless absolutely necessary. The former teammate's dare cuts to the heart of cricket's eternal debate: when does a legend's record earn patience, and when does it become a shield from accountability?

The Case for Rohit

Rohit's defenders point to his captaincy — under his leadership, India has maintained its position as the top-ranked ODI side and delivered consistent results across formats. His big-match temperament, tactical nous, and ability to set up totals with explosive starts remain assets that no young replacement can immediately replicate.

At his best, Rohit is a different class of opener — the kind who makes 264 against Sri Lanka or a century in a World Cup semifinal look routine. That ability doesn't vanish overnight.

The Case for Change

On the other side, young Indian batsmen are producing runs in domestic cricket and the IPL with a hunger that demands opportunity. India's deep batting talent pool means the team can afford transitions that other nations cannot. And history shows that even the greatest Indian batsmen — from Tendulkar to Dhoni — faced hard conversations about when to step aside.

The BCCI selectors face a familiar dilemma: manage a graceful transition that respects a champion's legacy while ensuring the team evolves. Getting it wrong in either direction — dropping him too early or too late — carries consequences for the team's results and the board's relationship with its most popular active player.

For now, Rohit Sharma remains India's captain across formats. Whether that changes will depend on runs, not rhetoric — no matter how bold the dare.
